title: Missing Number
summary: Figure-based puzzles — paired grids, single grids, circles — where one cell is hidden behind a numerical rule. Every rule connects the cells of a row (or segment), and the same rule is demonstrated by at least two complete instances. The winning habit is two-line verification: fit the rule on one complete row, confirm on the other, then apply. Digit-sum and digit-reversal variants reward students who switch families quickly when plain arithmetic stalls.

subtopics.title: How missing-number puzzles work
subtopics.concept: A figure hides one number with a '?'. The other parts of the figure follow one **hidden rule**. Find the rule from the complete rows, check it on every row, then use it once on the row with the '?'. Most rules are simple: add, multiply, square, or one small change on top.

formulas.name: Rule check
formulas.tex: f(a_1, b_1) = c_1 \text{ and } f(a_2, b_2) = c_2 \Rightarrow \text{use } f
formulas.note: One row fitting proves nothing. Two rows fitting is strong proof.

formulas.name: Common families
formulas.tex: a + b,\ a - b,\ ab,\ ab \pm k,\ (a + b)k,\ a^2 \pm b
formulas.note: Sums and products cover most puzzles. Try them first.

tricks.title: Test the spare row
tricks.body: Write your guessed rule as a formula. Test it on the second complete row. Only then use it on the row with the ?. This takes ten seconds and stops the most common wrong answer.

tricks.title: Build the biggest number first
tricks.body: Pick the biggest number in the row. Try to make it from the smaller ones. This finds the rule faster than reading left to right.

mistakes.wrong: Fitting a rule to the first row and answering at once.
mistakes.right: Test the rule on the second complete row before you use it.

mistakes.wrong: Reading the figure only left to right.
mistakes.right: The rule may run down a column or across opposite parts. Try those too.

mistakes.wrong: Using a three-step rule when a simple one exists.
mistakes.right: Real exam rules are short. Try add, multiply and square first.

mistakes.wrong: Picking the option that equals the plain product or plain square.
mistakes.right: That is often bait. Check that the plain rule really fits a complete row.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing the numbers of grid 1 with grid 2.
mistakes.right: Find the rule in one grid. Then apply it on the other grid.

subtopics.notes:
### What the puzzle looks like
A figure hides one number. It may be rows of numbers, two square grids, a circle or a triangle. Every complete part follows the **same rule**. Find it. Then use it once on the part with the "?".

Small example: 3 → 9, 4 → 16, 5 → ?. Each number is squared. So ? = 25.

> **Rule:** The rule is the same in every complete row. One row can fit a wrong rule by luck. Two rows almost never do.

### The rule ladder
Test simple rules first. Stop at the first rule that fits **all** the rows.

| Step | Rule to test | Sample with 4 and 7 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Add or subtract | 4 + 7 = 11 |
| 2 | Multiply | 4 × 7 = 28 |
| 3 | Multiply, then add or subtract a small number | 4 × 7 + 1 = 29 |
| 4 | Square, or square and adjust | $4^2 + 1 = 17$ |
| 5 | Digit tricks (sum, reverse) | see the digit lesson |

### Check every row
Rows: (3, 4, 13), (5, 2, 11), (6, 3, ?).

1. Try the sum. 3 + 4 = 7, not 13. Drop it.
2. Try the product. 3 × 4 = 12. The answer 13 is one more.
3. Guess: third = first × second + 1.
4. Test on row 2. 5 × 2 + 1 = 11. It fits.
5. Apply to row 3. 6 × 3 + 1 = **19**.

> **Tip:** Write the rule as a small formula, like c = a × b + 1. Then test that formula on the spare row.

### Start from the biggest number
The biggest number in a row is usually the answer of the rule. The smaller numbers are the inputs.

Ask: how do the small numbers build the big one? 26 comes from 5 as $5^2 + 1$. 21 comes from 4 and 5 as 4 × 5 + 1. Reading left to right hides the rule. Building the biggest number shows it.

### Read the size of the answer
Compare the answer with the inputs. This tells you which family to try.

| The answer is | Try first |
|---|---|
| About the sum of the inputs | Add or subtract |
| About the product | Multiply, then adjust |
| Close to a square number | Squares, like $a^2 \pm b$ |
| Smaller than both inputs | Difference, average or a digit rule |

### Two grids and one hole
Often two complete grids sit beside a grid with a "?". The rule works inside each grid, row by row.

1. Find the rule in grid 1.
2. Test it on grid 2. It must fit every row.
3. Apply it to the row with the "?".

Grid 1 rows: (2, 3, 7) and (3, 4, 13). Rule: a × b + 1. Grid 2 has (5, 6, 31). Check: 5 × 6 + 1 = 31. So (4, 5, ?) gives 4 × 5 + 1 = **21**.

### Wrong options are planted
The examiner puts the most tempting wrong answer in the options. If the rule is a × b + 1, the plain product is there as bait.

For row (6, 3, ?), the plain product is 18. The right answer is 19. If your answer matches a simpler version of the rule, test that simple rule on a complete row. It will fail.

> **Watch:** Never answer from one row. Two rows must agree.

patterns.name: Third number is a multiple of the first
patterns.howToSpot: Rows of two numbers. The second is a fixed multiple of the first, or a plain sum or difference.
steps: Divide the second number by the first in each row.
If the answer is the same, that is the multiplier.
Multiply the first number of the last row by it.
patterns.why: The simplest rules are tried first, and this one is the simplest.

patterns.name: Square of the number, then adjust
patterns.howToSpot: The answers sit close to perfect squares like 10, 17, 26 or 48.
steps: Square the first number in each row.
Find what is left over: add or subtract a number.
The leftover must be the same in every row.
patterns.why: A square with a small correction is a favourite exam rule.

patterns.name: Two grids, one rule
patterns.howToSpot: Two complete grids and a third grid with one missing cell.
steps: Find the row rule in grid 1.
Test it on grid 2. It must fit.
Use it on the row with the ?.
patterns.why: The second grid is a free check of the rule.

example.q: Grid 1 rows: (2, 3, 7) and (3, 4, 13). Grid 2 rows: (4, 5, ?) and (5, 6, 31). Find ?.

patterns.name: Two rules fit the first row
patterns.howToSpot: The first row fits more than one rule. Only a second row can choose between them.
steps: Write every rule that fits row 1.
Keep the rule that fits both rows.
Use it on the last row.
patterns.why: Setters build rows so that a wrong rule survives one row but not two.

steps: The rule is a × b. So 6 × 4 = 24.

patterns.name: Cube of the number, then adjust
patterns.howToSpot: The answers jump fast: 9, 28, 65. They sit next to cubes like 8, 27, 64.
steps: Cube the first number in each row.
Check the leftover. It must be the same in every row.
Apply the rule to the last row.
patterns.why: When answers grow faster than squares, a cube is the next family to try.

steps: $3^3 = 27$ and $4^3 = 64$. Both are 1 less than the answer.

patterns.name: Multiply, then add a number
patterns.howToSpot: Each answer is a little more than a multiple of the first number.
steps: Divide each answer by the first number to guess the multiplier.
The leftover gives the number to add.
Test on both rows, then apply.
patterns.why: Two small operations in a row are still a simple rule.

revision: Test rules in this order: add or subtract, multiply, multiply and adjust, squares, digit tricks.
The rule must fit every complete row. One fit is luck.
The biggest number in a row is usually the answer of the rule.
The size of the answer tells you the family: sum, product or square.
Two grids: find the rule in grid 1, test on grid 2, then apply it.
The plain product or plain square is often a planted wrong option.

subtopics.title: Grids with row (or column) rules
subtopics.concept: In a 3×3 grid, each row usually turns its first two numbers into the third with the same rule. Sometimes the rule runs down the columns instead. Find the rule on the complete rows, test it on every complete row, then fill the hole.

tricks.title: Build the biggest cell first
tricks.body: Write the biggest cell of a row. Rebuild it from the other two. This shows the rule faster than reading left to right.

tricks.title: Copy the grid as three rows
tricks.body: Write the grid as three lines in your rough space, with the ? in place. Reading numbers off the figure while you calculate leads to mistakes.

mistakes.wrong: Using grid 1's row rule on grid 2's columns.
mistakes.right: Use the same direction in every grid. Rows with rows, columns with columns.

mistakes.wrong: Picking between two half-fitting rules by feel.
mistakes.right: Test both rules on every complete row. Keep only the one that fits all.
Row 2 must fit too. A rule that fits one row is luck.

mistakes.wrong: Reading a column rule as a row rule.
mistakes.right: If no row rule fits, read the grid downwards.

subtopics.notes:
### What a grid puzzle looks like
A grid has three rows of three numbers. One cell is a "?". Each row follows the same rule.

Row (4, 6, 10): here 4 + 6 = 10. The first two numbers make the third. Your job is to find this link fast.

### Hunt for the link
Cover the third column. Ask how the first two numbers make the third. Try these in order.

1. Add or subtract: $a + b$, $a - b$.
2. Multiply: $ab$. Then $2ab$, $ab + k$, $ab - k$.
3. Squares: $a^2 + b$, $a^2 - b$, $a^2 + b^2$.
4. Square of a sum: $(a + b)^2$.
5. Sum times a number: $(a + b) \times k$.
6. Average: $\dfrac{a + b}{2}$.

> **Tip:** If the third number is a perfect square, like 25, 49 or 144, try a square rule first.

### Check every row
Rows: (4, 6, 10), (5, 3, 22), (7, 2, ?).

1. Sum: 4 + 6 = 10. It fits row 1. But 5 + 3 = 8, not 22. Drop it.
2. Product: 4 × 6 = 24, not 10. Drop it.
3. Try $a^2 - b$. Row 1: 16 − 6 = 10. Row 2: 25 − 3 = 22. Both fit.
4. Apply: 49 − 2 = **47**.

> **Watch:** Stopping at row 1 would give 7 + 2 = 9. That is the planted wrong option. Always test the second row.

### When rows fail, try columns
If no row rule fits, read the grid downwards. The third row may come from the first two rows, cell by cell.

Rows: (2, 3, 5), (4, 5, 6), (8, 15, ?). Check the columns: 2 × 4 = 8 and 3 × 5 = 15. So the third row is first row × second row. Then ? = 5 × 6 = **30**.

The middle cell can also be the average of the outer cells. In (10, 14, 18) and (22, 25, 28), the middle number is the average. So (30, ?, 40) gives 35.

### Sum, then a multiplier
Sometimes the third number is a multiple of the sum. Add the first two numbers. Then divide the third number by that sum.

Rows: (4, 7, 22) and (6, 3, 18). Row 1: 4 + 7 = 11, and 22 ÷ 11 = 2. Row 2: 6 + 3 = 9, and 18 ÷ 9 = 2. The multiplier is 2 in both rows. So (9, 5, ?) gives 14 × 2 = **28**.

### Circles and triangles
Match parts by position.

- Circle: opposite parts often share a total. Pairs 12–8 and 15–5 both add to 20. So 18 pairs with 2.
- Triangle: the centre may be the sum or product of the corners. Corners 2, 3, 4 give centre 24. Corners 1, 5, 3 give 15. So corners 2, 6, 3 give 36.

Write each matched set as a small sum. Look for the same link in every set.

### Two complete grids
The rule stays the same in both grids. Only the numbers change. Solve the left grid, check it on the middle grid, then use it on the last grid.

### Speed helps
- Learn squares up to 25.
- Use $a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)$ to skip big squares: $7^2 - 3^2 = 10 \times 4 = 40$.
- Build the biggest cell first: $22 = (4 + 7) \times 2$.

> **Rule:** One rule, every row, then answer.

patterns.name: Row sums and differences
patterns.howToSpot: The third number is close to the sum or difference of the first two.
steps: Test c = a + b on every row.
If it fails, test the difference a − b.
Use the rule that fits every row.
patterns.why: Adding is the most common way to build a grid.

patterns.name: Squares added together
patterns.howToSpot: The third number is much bigger than the first two, and it is a perfect square.
patterns.why: Square rules make the third number too big for a plain sum or product.

patterns.name: Column rules
patterns.howToSpot: No row rule fits. The grid may work downwards.
steps: Test third row = first row + second row, cell by cell.
Then test the product of the two rows.
Confirm on every complete column, then fill the hole.
patterns.why: The setter sometimes turns the rule to run down the columns.

steps: The third row is first row × second row.

patterns.name: Circle and triangle figures
patterns.howToSpot: Numbers sit around a circle, or at the corners of a triangle with a centre.
steps: Pair opposite parts of the circle. Test a fixed sum, then a fixed product.
For a triangle, test centre = sum or product of the corners.
patterns.why: These figures repeat one link across matched parts.

example.q: A circle has opposite pairs 12 and 8, 15 and 5, and 18 and ?. Find ?.

patterns.name: Multiply, then add or subtract a number
patterns.howToSpot: The third number is a little more or less than the product of the first two.
steps: Multiply the first two numbers in each row.
Find what is left over. It must be the same in every row.
patterns.why: A small change on a product is the most used disguise for multiplying.

patterns.name: Sum, then multiply by a number
patterns.howToSpot: The third number is even, or a multiple of a fixed number, and bigger than the sum.
steps: Divide the third number by that sum.
The quotient k must be the same in every row.
patterns.why: Adding first and then scaling is a common two-step rule.

patterns.name: Square of the first, minus the second
patterns.howToSpot: The third number is close to the square of the first number.
steps: Subtract the third number from the square. The result should be the second number.
patterns.why: Squares with a subtraction often hide behind large third numbers.

revision: Try in order: sum or difference, product, squares, (a + b)², sum times a number, average.
The rule must fit every complete row, and the second grid too.
Rows fail: try columns. Circles: opposite parts. Triangles: centre and corners.
Third numbers that are perfect squares point to a square rule.
Build the biggest cell from the others.
Learn squares up to 25. Use a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).

subtopics.title: Digit-sum and digit-reversal rules
subtopics.concept: Some puzzles work on the **digits** of the numbers, not on their values. The rule may add the digits of each number, reverse the digits, or multiply the digits. Try a digit rule when ordinary sums and products do not fit.

formulas.name: Digit sum
formulas.note: Add the digits of the number.

formulas.name: Reversal
formulas.note: Write the digits in the opposite order.

formulas.name: Digit product
formulas.note: Multiply the digits of the number.

tricks.title: Switch to digits when standard rules fail
tricks.body: Give ordinary rules about 30 seconds. If both complete rows refuse them, test these in order: digit sums, reverse of the sum, digit sums plus a number.

steps: Row 1: 10 + 9 = 19, and 21 is 2 more. Row 2: 9 + 5 = 14, and 16 is 2 more.

tricks.title: Add first, then flip
tricks.body: A reversal answer must read backwards cleanly. Add the two numbers first, then reverse the sum. Confirm on two rows.

mistakes.wrong: Reversing the inputs when the rule reverses the sum.
mistakes.right: Test both orders on a complete row. Use the one that fits.

mistakes.wrong: Slipping on digit sums of numbers with 0 or repeated digits.
mistakes.right: Write each digit sum in a short line, like 40 → 4 + 0 = 4.

mistakes.wrong: Skipping the second-row check because the rule looks digital.
Adding the digits of the numbers when the rule adds first, then sums the digits.
mistakes.right: Test S(a) + S(b) and S(a + b). They differ when there is a carry.

mistakes.wrong: Changing to another variant for the last row.
mistakes.right: Use the same variant that fitted the complete rows.

subtopics.notes:
### When the rule uses digits
Some rows look odd because the values do not match: 28, 9, 21. Adding the digits explains it: 2 + 8 = 10, then 10 + 9 + 2 = 21.

Three digit tools cover most puzzles. Learn their short names.

| Tool | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $S(n)$ | sum of the digits | $S(47) = 4 + 7 = 11$ |
| $R(n)$ | digits reversed | $R(43) = 34$ |
| $P(n)$ | product of the digits | $P(47) = 4 \times 7 = 28$ |

### Digit-sum rules
The answer is small, but the numbers are two-digit. Try these:

- $S(a) + S(b)$: 47 and 38 give 11 + 11 = 22.
- $S(a + b)$: add first, then sum the digits. 68 gives 14.
- A digit sum times a number, like $S(a) \times b$.

Test one variant on a complete row. Then test it on the next row. Only one variant fits all.

### Reversal rules
Look for mirror pairs, like 43 and 34.

- $R(a) + R(b)$: reverse both numbers, then add. 34 + 41 = 75.
- $R(a + b)$: add first, then reverse the sum. 39 becomes 93.

> **Tip:** Reversing first and adding first can give different answers. Test both on a row where the digits carry over.

### Digit-product rules
The answer is very small. Multiply the digits of each number.

$P(24) = 2 \times 4 = 8$ and $P(35) = 15$. So $P(47) = 28$.

> **Watch:** A number with a 0, like 40 or 10, has a digit product of 0. This usually rules out a product rule at once.

### A full walk-through
Rows: (39, 25, 10), (57, 18, 12), (68, 26, ?).

1. Plain sum: 39 + 25 = 64, not 10. Drop it.
2. Digit sums added: 3 + 9 = 12 and 2 + 5 = 7. Total 19, not 10. Drop it.
3. Add first, then take the digit sum: 64 gives 6 + 4 = 10. It fits.
4. Test row 2: 57 + 18 = 75, and 7 + 5 = 12. It fits.
5. Apply: 68 + 26 = 94, and 9 + 4 = **13**.

### How to spot a digit rule
- The answers are far too small or too big for plain sums and products.
- The answers are near 5 to 30 while the numbers are two-digit.
- The same digits appear again and again: 43 and 34, or 62 and 26.

### A quick check with 9
A number and its digit sum leave the same remainder when divided by 9. This helps to check a digit-sum answer. For example 47 + 38 = 85, and $S(47) + S(38) = 22$. Both 85 and 22 leave remainder 4.

### Add a fixed number
Sometimes the digit sums are close but always short by the same amount. Rows (28, 9, 21) and (36, 23, 16) show it. The digit sums total 19 and 14. The answers are 2 more each time. So the rule is $S(a) + S(b) + 2$.

### Reversal with a zero
- Reversing the inputs when the rule reverses the sum, or the other way round.
- A sum that ends in 0, like 40. Reversal gives 04 = 4. Setters avoid this. If you see it, you may have the wrong rule.

> **Rule:** Use the same variant that fitted the complete rows. Do not switch to another one for the last row.

patterns.name: Sum of the digit sums
patterns.howToSpot: The answers are small (5 to 30) while the numbers are two-digit.
steps: Find S(a) and S(b) for each row.
Add them and compare with the third number.
patterns.why: Digit sums shrink big numbers to answer-sized ones.

patterns.name: Reverse each number, then add
patterns.howToSpot: Digits mirror across the row, like 43 beside 34.
steps: Confirm on every row, then apply.
patterns.why: Reversal is the most reused digit trick.

patterns.name: Product of the digits
patterns.howToSpot: The answers are tiny, even smaller than the digit sums.
steps: Multiply the digits of the first number.
patterns.why: Digit products shrink numbers even more than digit sums.

patterns.name: Digit sum times the other number
patterns.howToSpot: One number is shrunk by its digit sum. The other stays whole.
steps: Find the digit sum of the first number.
Multiply it by the second number.
patterns.why: Mixing a digit tool with a plain number hides the rule one level deeper.

patterns.name: Add first, then reverse the sum
patterns.howToSpot: The answers are mirror images of the row sums, like sum 42 and answer 24.
steps: Reverse the digits of the sum.
Confirm on a second row. Then apply.
patterns.why: The reverse is applied to the result, not to the inputs.

patterns.name: Digit sum of the total
patterns.howToSpot: Adding the digit sums separately does not fit, but the digit sum of the total does.
steps: Then find the digit sum of the total.
Check S(a) + S(b) too. It differs when there is a carry.
patterns.why: Adding before or after taking digit sums gives different answers when digits carry over.

patterns.name: Digit sums plus a fixed number
patterns.howToSpot: The digit sums are close to the answer but a small fixed amount is left over.
steps: Add the digit sums of both numbers.
Find the leftover to reach the answer.
The leftover must be the same in every row.
patterns.why: A fixed add-on is a small extra step on the digit-sum rule.

revision: S(n) is the digit sum, R(n) reverses the digits, P(n) multiplies the digits.
Common rules: S(a) + S(b), S(a + b), R(a) + R(b), R(a + b), P(a), S(a) × b.
Test each variant on a complete row. Only one fits all the rows.
Answers far smaller than the numbers point to a digit rule.
Mirror pairs like 43 and 34 point to reversal.
A 0 in a number kills a digit-product rule.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A 3×3 grid with one missing cell; rows (or columns) share a hidden rule.
pyqPatterns.approach: Test bridges in order: a+b, |a−b|, ab, 2ab, ab±k, a²+b², (a+b)² — fit on every complete row before applying.

example.solution: Plain a+b fails (9, 12). Divide out: 15 = 5×3, 28 = 7×4 — the multipliers 5, 7 are one less than the first numbers → c = (a−1)×b → (9−1)×5 = **40**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two complete grids and an incomplete third.
pyqPatterns.approach: Derive the rule on the first grid, verify it on the second, then apply to the third.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Output cells sit next to perfect squares (26, 48, 50, 63...).
pyqPatterns.approach: Square the first (or second) input and read the leftover: a² ± b, a² ± 1, a² + b².

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Numbers placed in sectors of a circle or corners of a triangle with a centre value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Treat each sector as a row, or pair opposite sectors; test constant sum, then centre = sum/product of corners.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Mirror-image digits across the row (23 beside 32); outputs look like scrambled sums.
pyqPatterns.approach: Test R(a) + R(b) and R(a + b); confirm on both complete rows.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Outputs are small and factor neatly into the digits of the inputs.
pyqPatterns.approach: P(n) = product of digits; test P(a), P(a) + P(b), then weighted mixtures.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Third numbers tiny compared with the values.
pyqPatterns.approach: S(a)+S(b) first, then S(a+b); fit on all complete rows.

solvedExamples.q:
Study the pattern and find the missing number.

**Grid 1:** 7, 9, 4  **Grid 2:** 8, 5, 7  **Grid 3:** 11, 3, ?

(In each grid, the numbers are read left to right as one row.)
solvedExamples.solution: Test the row rule on both complete grids: 7 + 9 + 4 = 20 and 8 + 5 + 7 = 20 — the **row sum is always 20**. So 11 + 3 + ? = 20 → ? = **6**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add a complete row; if two complete rows share the same total, the rule is 'sum = constant'.

solvedExamples.solution: Each row: third = first × second. Check: 4×3 = 12 ✓; 5×4 = 20 ✓. So 7 × 2 = **14**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: The largest cell factorises neatly into the other two — test the product rule first.
solvedExamples.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

solvedExamples.solution: Plain sums fail (42 ≠ 24 as a value... but 24 is 42 reversed). Rule: **reverse the digits of (first + second)**. Check: 24+18 = 42 → 24 ✓; 32+13 = 45 → 54 ✓. So 26+15 = 41 → reversed = **14**. (41 is the unreversed sum — the planted trap.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: When sums 'almost' match, check whether the third cell is the reversed sum.

solvedExamples.solution: Digit-sum rule: third = digit-sum(first) + digit-sum(second) + 2. Check: 10 + 9 + 2 = 21 ✓; 9 + 5 + 2 = 16 ✓. So 9 + 8 + 2 = **19**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Sums/products fail → add the digits of each number, then look for the constant.

practice.solution: Rule: third = first × second + 1. Check: 3×4 + 1 = 13 ✓; 5×2 + 1 = 11 ✓. So 6×3 + 1 = **19**. (18 is the bare product — the near-miss trap.)
practice.shortcut: Product first, then look for the small constant: +1 here.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: Rule: third = first − second. Check: 9−2 = 7 ✓; 12−5 = 7 ✓. So 15 − 9 = **6**. (7 repeats in the first two rows — do not copy it into the third.)
practice.shortcut: Same answer twice in a row is a coincidence trap; always derive, never pattern-copy.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: 22 = (4+7)×2; confirm 18 = (6+3)×2 ✓. Rule: third = (first + second) × 2. So (9+5)×2 = **28**. (45 is 9×5 — the product trap.)
practice.shortcut: Large third cell with modest inputs → try (a+b)×k or a×b first.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.shortcut: When a×b overshoots (30 vs 15), test a×(b−1) or b×(a−1) — the 'one less' family.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: Digit sums: 29 → 11, 14 → 5; 11 + 5 = 16 and 18 − 16 = 2. Confirm: 38 → 11, 25 → 7; 11 + 7 + 2 = 20 ✓. Rule: third = digitsum(first) + digitsum(second) + 2. So 11 + 4 + 2 = **17**.
practice.shortcut: Standard rules dead for two seconds → switch to digit sums and find the constant.

practice.solution: 49 = 8² − 15; confirm 39 = 7² − 10 = 49 − 10 ✓. Rule: third = (first)² − second. So 6² − 11 = 36 − 11 = **25**. (36 is 6² without subtracting 11.)
practice.shortcut: The third number sits just below the square of the first (49 is 8² = 64 minus 15), so test a² − b: 6² − 11 = **25**.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: 10 = (12+8) ÷ 2; confirm 13 = (20+6) ÷ 2 = 26 ÷ 2 ✓. Rule: third = average of first two. So (14+4) ÷ 2 = **9**. (18 is the un-divided sum.)
practice.shortcut: Third cell sitting between the other two → test their average.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: 25 = 5×(6−1); confirm 21 = 7×(4−1) ✓. Rule: third = first × (second − 1). So 9 × (3−1) = **18**. (27 = 9×3 is the bare product.)
practice.shortcut: a×b too big by exactly a (or b) → the second factor carries a −1.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: In each row, third column = first + second: 6+5 = 11 ✓; 9+4 = 13 ✓. So 8 + 7 = **15**. (56 = 8×7 is the product trap.)
practice.shortcut: Column-wise rule — read each row as (a, b, a+b); the check rows confirm instantly.
practice.pattern: column rule in a single grid

practice.q:
Numbers are given in segments of a circular figure, each segment read as (outer, inner, centre):

**15   12   12**

**20   11   36**

**17    9    ?**
practice.solution: 12 = (15−12)×4; confirm 36 = (20−11)×4 = 9×4 ✓. Rule: centre = (outer − inner) × 4. So (17−9)×4 = **32**. (36 repeats the previous centre — a copy trap.)
practice.shortcut: Small centres from big outers → difference × constant is the natural family.

practice.solution: 43 + 14 = 57 → reversed = 75 ✓; 34 + 43 = 77 → reversed = 77 ✓. Rule: third = reverse(first + second). So 26 + 15 = 41 → **14**. (41, 51, 62 are the sum and the reversed inputs — all traps.)
practice.shortcut: Palindrome check row (77 → 77) is the giveaway that reversal is involved.

practice.solution: 31 = 45 − 14 = 9×5 − (9+5); confirm 34 = 48 − 14 = 8×6 − (8+6) ✓. Rule: third = product − sum. So 40 − 14 = **26**. (40 is the bare product.)
practice.shortcut: Constant 14 = a+b in both rows — subtract the sum from the product.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: Third = first + second: 4 + 9 = 13 and 7 + 6 = 13. So 5 + 8 = **13**. The repeated 13s tempt you to copy — derive it; the rule happens to give 13 again, but only the derivation proves it. (40 = 5×8 is the product trap.)
practice.shortcut: When every third cell matches, verify the sum rule before trusting a copy.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: 64 = 100 − 36 = 10² − 6²; confirm 128 = 144 − 16 = 12² − 4² ✓. Rule: third = a² − b². So 81 − 25 = **56**. (45 = 9×5 is the product trap; 70 and 85 come from slipping the squares.)
practice.shortcut: Both inputs squaring cleanly and a big third cell → a² − b².
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.shortcut: ab + a + b factorises as (a+1)(b+1) − 1 — a fast mental identity.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: Second number = 4 × first: 3 × 4 = 12 ✓, 7 × 4 = 28 ✓. So 9 × 4 = **36**. (27 uses ×3, which fits neither row.)
practice.shortcut: Divide the output by the input — a constant quotient means a constant multiplier.

practice.solution: a + b gives 7 and 7, not 10 and 12 — the first number counts twice. Rule: third = 2 × first + second: 6 + 4 = 10 ✓, 10 + 2 = 12 ✓. So 12 + 5 = **17**. (16 doubles the wrong number.)
practice.shortcut: Output just above a + b by exactly one input → that input is doubled.

practice.solution: Sum and product both fail (9, 20 against 11). Rule: third = 3 × first − second: 15 − 4 = 11 ✓, 18 − 2 = 16 ✓. So 24 − 3 = **21**. (24 forgets to subtract the second number.)
practice.shortcut: Output between a and 3a → try ka ± b.

practice.solution: 10 = 3² + 1 and 37 = 6² + 1. So 8² + 1 = **65**. (64 is the bare square — the near-miss.)
practice.shortcut: Outputs one above a perfect square → a² + 1.

practice.solution: 19 = 4² + 3 and 9 = 2² + 5 — the SECOND number is squared. Rule: third = second² + first. So 5² + 6 = **31**. (41 squares the wrong number: 6² + 5.)
practice.shortcut: Try squaring each input in turn; only one choice fits both rows.

practice.solution: 25 and 36 are perfect squares: 25 = (2 + 3)², 36 = (4 + 2)². Rule: third = (first + second)². So (3 + 5)² = **64**. (34 = 3² + 5² squares separately.)
practice.shortcut: Every output a perfect square → find what is being squared.

practice.q:
Study the pattern and find the missing number.

**Grid 1:** 3, 5, 16  **Grid 2:** 4, 6, 25  **Grid 3:** 5, 7, ?

(Each grid is read left to right as one row.)
practice.solution: Grid 1: 3 × 5 + 1 = 16; grid 2 confirms: 4 × 6 + 1 = 25 ✓. Grid 3: 5 × 7 + 1 = **36**. (35 is the bare product.)
practice.shortcut: Solve grid 1, confirm on grid 2, apply to grid 3.

practice.q:
Study the pattern and find the missing number.

**Grid 1:** 6, 4, 18  **Grid 2:** 5, 7, 30  **Grid 3:** 8, 3, ?

(Each grid is read left to right as one row.)
practice.solution: Products 24 and 35 overshoot by exactly the first number (6 and 5). Rule: third = first × (second − 1): 6 × 3 = 18 ✓, 5 × 6 = 30 ✓. So 8 × 2 = **16**. (21 = 3 × 7 reduces the wrong factor.)
practice.shortcut: Product too big by one input → that input's partner carries a −1.

practice.q:
Study the pattern and find the missing number.

**Grid 1:** 8, 9, 8  **Grid 2:** 12, 6, 7  **Grid 3:** 10, 4, ?

(Each grid is read left to right as one row.)
practice.solution: No clean a-to-c bridge exists, so total the rows: 8 + 9 + 8 = 25 and 12 + 6 + 7 = 25. Every grid sums to 25 → 10 + 4 + ? = 25 → ? = **11**.
practice.shortcut: When bridges fail, add each complete row — equal totals mean a constant-sum rule.

practice.solution: Row 1 tempts with 2 + 4 = 6, but row 2 gives 5 + 3 = 8 ≠ 13 — the sum rule dies. Product − 2 fits both: 8 − 2 = 6 ✓, 15 − 2 = 13 ✓. So 24 − 2 = **22**. (10 is the sum rule that only fitted row 1.)
practice.shortcut: A rule that fits one row is a coincidence until the second row agrees.

practice.solution: Row 1 looks like a product (2 × 4 = 8), but row 2 breaks it (5 × 3 = 15 ≠ 28). Rule: first² + second: 4 + 4 = 8 ✓, 25 + 3 = 28 ✓. So 36 + 2 = **38**. (12 is the product rule; 34 subtracts instead of adding.)
practice.shortcut: Test the second row before trusting the first.

practice.solution: The multipliers differ (×3, then ×6), so no constant multiple fits. 12 = 4² − 4 and 42 = 7² − 7 ✓. So 9² − 9 = **72**. (81 is the bare square; 36 = 9 × 4 copies row 1's ×3 idea.)
practice.shortcut: Changing multiplier equal to (a − 1) → a × (a − 1) = a² − a.

practice.solution: Third = first − second: 15 − 7 = 8 ✓, 20 − 9 = 11 ✓. So 18 − 5 = **13**. (23 adds instead.)
practice.shortcut: Output smaller than the first input → subtraction.

practice.solution: Sums are 14 and 16; the outputs are 11 and 13 — always 3 less. Rule: third = first + second − 3. So 11 − 3 = **8**. (11 is the bare sum; 1 is the difference.)
practice.shortcut: Constant gap between output and a + b → a + b ± k.

practice.solution: Products are 12 and 10; outputs are exactly double. Rule: third = 2 × first × second. So 2 × 24 = **48**. (24 is the undoubled product.)
practice.shortcut: Output ÷ product constant → k × ab.

practice.solution: 5 = 1² + 2² and 29 = 2² + 5² ✓. Rule: third = first² + second². So 9 + 36 = **45**. (81 = (3 + 6)² squares the sum instead.)
practice.shortcut: Output neither sum nor product but beats both → sum of squares.

practice.solution: The missing cell is in the middle, so read each row as (left, middle, right): 9 = (6 + 12) ÷ 2 ✓, 20 = (15 + 25) ÷ 2 ✓. Middle = average of the outer two → (8 + 20) ÷ 2 = **14**. (28 forgets to halve.)
practice.shortcut: A middle cell sitting between its neighbours → average.

practice.solution: Rows resist every bridge (4, 7 → 3 but 5, 2 → 9). Read down the columns instead: 4 + 5 = 9 ✓, 7 + 2 = 9 ✓ — the bottom row is the sum of the two above. So 3 + 9 = **12**. (18 = 9 + 9 is a row-wise guess.)
practice.shortcut: Rows stuck → try columns: bottom = top ± middle, cell by cell.

practice.q: Numbers are written in the six sectors of a circle. Reading opposite sectors as pairs: **14 – 9**, **11 – 12**, **16 – ?**. Find the missing number.
practice.solution: Each opposite pair sums to the same total: 14 + 9 = 23, 11 + 12 = 23. So 16 + ? = 23 → ? = **7**. (9 copies a neighbour; 25 is 16 + 9.)
practice.shortcut: Opposite sectors → constant sum (or product) first.

practice.q:
In each triangle the corners are (left, right, top) and a number sits in the centre:

**(2, 3, 4) → 20**

**(1, 5, 3) → 18**

**(4, 2, 5) → ?**
practice.solution: Product of corners fails (24 ≠ 20), sum fails (9). Rule: centre = (left + right) × top: (2 + 3) × 4 = 20 ✓, (1 + 5) × 3 = 18 ✓. So (4 + 2) × 5 = **30**. (40 is the product of all three corners.)
practice.shortcut: Centre just below the corner product → try (x + y) × z.

practice.solution: Outputs are far too small for sums of values → digit sums. S(23) + S(41) = 5 + 5 = 10 ✓; S(27) + S(45) = 9 + 9 = 18 ✓. So S(35) + S(26) = 8 + 8 = **16**. (61 is the plain sum.)
practice.shortcut: Two-digit inputs, small outputs → add all the digits.

practice.solution: Adding digit sums separately fails (11 + 9 = 20 ≠ 11). Add first, then sum the digits: 38 + 27 = 65 → 11 ✓; 54 + 18 = 72 → 9 ✓. So 46 + 37 = 83 → 8 + 3 = **11**. (20 is the separate digit-sum trap.)
practice.shortcut: Carries make S(a+b) differ from S(a)+S(b) — test both.

practice.solution: S(12) = 3, S(31) = 4 → 3 × 4 = 12 ✓; S(22) = 4, S(15) = 6 → 24 ✓. Rule: product of digit sums. So S(41) × S(23) = 5 × 5 = **25**. (10 adds the digit sums.)
practice.shortcut: Digit sums that multiply to the output → S(a) × S(b).

practice.solution: Reverse each input, then add: 21 + 32 = 53 ✓; 13 + 41 = 54 ✓. So 12 + 23 = **35**. (53 adds the unreversed inputs — which is exactly row 1's output, a planted trap.)
practice.shortcut: Outputs look like sums of flipped numbers → reverse first.

practice.solution: 25 + 17 = 42 → reversed 24 ✓; 38 + 16 = 54 → reversed 45 ✓. Rule: reverse the sum. So 19 + 33 = 52 → **25**. (52 forgets to reverse; 124 reverses the inputs instead: 91 + 33.)
practice.shortcut: Sum first, flip second.

practice.solution: Plain difference fails (52 − 13 = 39). Reverse the first number, then subtract: 25 − 13 = 12 ✓; 17 − 9 = 8 ✓. So 38 − 20 = **18**. (63 = 83 − 20 skips the reversal; 36 reverses the difference instead.)
practice.shortcut: Reverse only the two-digit input when the other is small.

practice.solution: 8 = 2 × 4 and 18 = 3 × 6 — multiply the digits. So 5 × 7 = **35**. (12 adds the digits.)
practice.shortcut: Output = digit product: check with the first pair.

practice.solution: Digit sums give 9, not 10, for row 1 — try digit products: 6 + 4 = 10 ✓; 6 + 10 = 16 ✓. So P(43) + P(62) = 12 + 12 = **24**. (15 adds digit sums; 144 multiplies the two products.)
practice.shortcut: Digit sums miss by a little → switch to digit products.

practice.solution: S(13) × 5 = 4 × 5 = 20 ✓; S(42) × 3 = 6 × 3 = 18 ✓. Rule: digit sum of the first × second. So 6 × 4 = **24**. (204 multiplies the raw values; 10 adds instead of multiplying.)
practice.shortcut: Small second input + two-digit first → shrink the first, keep the second.

practice.solution: S(25) = 7 → 2 × 7 + 4 = 18 ✓; S(31) = 4 → 2 × 4 + 6 = 14 ✓. Rule: twice the first number's digit sum plus the second. So 2 × 11 + 3 = **25**. (14 forgets to double; 22 forgets the + second.)
practice.shortcut: Output − second number is even and small → 2 × digit sum.
